children.text: "Congratulations, your visa is approved!" — these are the words every US visa applicant longs to hear. A refusal, naturally, is associated with negative emotions and often confusion as well.

The decision on whether or not to grant a visa is made directly by the consular officer, who must decide within a few minutes whether the applicant is entitled to a visa. Accordingly, most cases are resolved based on the brief interview and a review of the ties and supporting documentation presented by the applicant. As for a refusal, the consul denies a US visa under section 214(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), under which every foreign national is presumed to be an intending immigrant until they demonstrate to the consular officer, at the time of application, that they are entitled to non-immigrant status.

Being refused a US non-immigrant visa once does not mean a subsequent refusal is guaranteed; accordingly, if you receive a negative decision, you have the option to submit a new application. Unfortunately, many applicants believe that a refusal received once is permanent, which is entirely untrue. So if you've received a refusal for a US visa once or several times, don't give up - every new application is a new chance. Below, we'll go into detail on how to increase your chances of a successful application.

page.title: About refusal under the US visa's Immigration and Nationality Act, section 214(b)

children.text: If you receive a refusal, you'll need to go through all the same steps you went through before. First, you organize your profile - if this time you want to have your interview in a different country, you'll need to transfer your existing profile to the country where you plan to schedule your interview; otherwise, transferring the profile isn't necessary. After that, you pay the visa fee, complete the application, and schedule your interview date.

After receiving a refusal, a question the consul often asks is what has changed in your case between interviews. That's exactly why, before scheduling another interview, it's better to let some time pass, so that you can make certain changes to your situation and give the consul a solid answer.

page.title: What should you consider in the event of a refusal?

children.text: As we already mentioned, after a refusal, you need to show the consul at your next interview all the changes that have taken place in your case. Before reapplying, answering the following questions may help:
What have I changed in my case since I received the refusal?
Did I explain my situation correctly?
Did the consular officer miss anything?
Is there additional information I can present to demonstrate my residence abroad and my strong ties?

The concept of strong ties varies by country, city, and individual. Ties can include your job, home, family, and bank account. "Ties" refer to the various aspects of your life that anchor you to your home country: property, employment, and social and family relationships. It's possible the consul didn't see sufficient ties, which is why they made a negative decision — so it's best to place special emphasis on the circumstances that will bring you back to your home country. You can also write down what ties you have that entitle you to a visa, which may not have been properly assessed during your interview with the consular officer. In the event of a refusal, you should also review the documents you presented for consideration by the consul.
In short, submitting a new visa application is always worthwhile - what matters most is being properly prepared, knowing your case well, and being ready to answer the questions the consul might ask.

If you've received a negative decision on your visa multiple times and think you need the help of a professional team with the process, fill out the registration form, and our team will contact you shortly.
